newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Public power on guard in open market debate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Public power on guard in open market debate.

text.p: Public power systems are zealously guarding their turf against lawmakers who might consider taking away their tax benefits in moves to open all local electricity markets to competition.

Although a quarter of all electricity in the United States is supplied by public power systems, legislation introduced to date in Congress to make states deregulate all power sales would not force public power to compete.
But energy providers and companies pressing for an open market say public power must be included in the deregulated market to give consumers a wide array of power supply choices.

"All that's being debated is whether today's public power consumers -- like the consumers now served by private power companies -- should be able to obtain the benefits of the competitive generation market," said Dick Munson, executive director of the Northeast-Midwest Institute, a non-profit research group.
A workshop held by the Senate Energy Committee this week showed that the battle to level the playing field will complicate the deregulation of electricity markets.
"It makes it more challenging," said Tim Brown, spokesman for the Electric Power Supply Association, which represents independent power producers.

Investor-owned utilities say it would be unfair to let federal, state and locally-owned power providers maintain their monopolies while all other power producers are forced to compete for market share.

At the same time, the private utilities say if federal, state, and local power groups are allowed to compete in an open market by selling outside their territories, they should lose their tax-exempt status.

"Tax-exempt financing by electric municipalities ... if allowed to continue unchecked predictably will seriously compromise free and open competition," said Dick Snell, chairman of Pinnacle West Capital Corp, which owns Arizona Public Service Corp.
Among the public power systems are some of the nation's biggest utilities, including the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power and the New York Power Authority.
Public power systems like those pay no federal, state or local income taxes and raise capital by issuing bonds with tax-exempt interest.

Under current tax rules, because public power groups have easier access to debt financing than private utilities, they are barred from selling more than 10 percent of their power or transmission capacity to other power providers.
The Internal Revenue Service is in the process of reviewing the rules in light of the changing market, but investor-owned utilities say Congress should act first.
Public power groups, including rural electric cooperatives, argue that if they lose their tax benefits, investor-owned utilites should give up their standard corporate tax breaks too.
At stake would be tax deferrals that investor-owned utilities enjoy, which the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, citing federal studies, said were worth $5 billion a year.

Public power groups call the deferred taxes interest-free loans, because utilities collect money from their ratepayers to cover their tax burden but end up keeping the money thanks to investment tax credits and depreciation benefits.
